memory_update.text: MRCY should remain in the underfollowed defense-electronics lane as a candidate for RF/microwave, rugged compute, secure processing, and embedded sensor-processing chokepoints; later layers must distinguish recurring production content from lower-quality development revenue.

DCO should remain in the underfollowed lane as a qualified aerospace/defense electronic systems and complex assembly supplier, especially if Electronic Systems exposure to missile, radar, classified, fixed-wing, and space programs continues to grow.

Potential speculative-shadow candidates not included due to the three-name cap: CODA for real-time 3D/4D/5D/6D subsea imaging sonar and defense/autonomous underwater situational awareness; future pass should verify market cap, defense revenue mix, customer concentration, and whether it sits below the USD 300M exception threshold.

For this node, the most important falsification question is whether the company owns a hard-to-replace qualified component/subsystem position, or whether it is simply a contract manufacturer with limited pricing power and many substitutes.

node: Aerospace and defense-qualified electronics, sensors, RF components, rugged compute, and precision subsystems
summary: Layer 1B expansion for the defense/aerospace-qualified electronics node. The reference lane uses L3Harris as a context anchor for demand in electronic warfare, resilient communications, space sensors, missile solutions, and defense electronics. The underfollowed lane surfaces Mercury Systems and Ducommun as smaller public suppliers with plausible chokepoint characteristics: qualified electronics, RF/microwave or rugged processing content, high-reliability manufacturing, and exposure to missile, radar, electronic warfare, military aircraft, classified, and space programs. These are research candidates only, not buy/sell recommendations. Key unresolved issue: whether program exposure translates into constrained, hard-to-substitute content versus merely being one of several qualified suppliers.
